summary: Describes a way to spread a Next Hop Resolution Protocol service over several servers within a Logical IP Subnet, using the Server Cache Synchronization Protocol to keep them in agreement.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of one helper answering all questions, several helpers share the work and tell each other what they know.

questions: what is a server group in nhrp
what is the scsp protocol id for nhrp
how does an nhrp client leave a server group
subtitle: How several NHRP servers in one subnet keep their client databases in step using SCSP.

tldr.problem: A Logical IP Subnet can have several NHRP Servers, and clients do not register with all of them, yet every client must be able to query at least one server about any client in the subnet.
tldr.mechanism: The Server Cache Synchronization Protocol (SCSP) keeps the servers' databases in agreement. This RFC supplies the NHRP-specific part: the layout of the cache record that SCSP carries and the values for the protocol-independent fields.
tldr.outcome: A client registers with one server but may use any server in the group. The RFC also sets rules for how a client leaves the group safely.

today: RFC 2335 is a Proposed Standard from April 1998, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the NHRP-specific companion to SCSP in RFC 2334.

sections.title: The Synchronization Problem
sections.content:
NHRP Clients (NHCs) register their existence and reachability with NHRP Servers (NHSs). A Logical IP Subnet (LIS) may have several NHSs. Clients need not register with all of them, but every client must be able to query at least one NHS about any client in the LIS. The databases of the servers therefore have to be synchronized across the LIS.

The Server Cache Synchronization Protocol (SCSP, RFC 2334) solves the generalized server synchronization problem for distributed databases. It has a protocol-independent part, defined in RFC 2334, and a client/server protocol specific part. This document specifies the second part, with NHRP (RFC 2332) as the client/server protocol. It is separate so that it could progress independently of the protocol-independent specification. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: Several helpers each keep a list of who is where. They must all keep the same list, and a standard way of sharing updates does that job.

sections.title: Server Groups and Client Registration
sections.content:
All NHSs in a LIS form a Server Group (SG). The group is identified by its SGID, carried in every SCSP packet. Every SCSP packet also has a Protocol ID (PID) field, which is set to 0x0002 to show that SCSP is synchronizing NHS databases. The RFC notes that this PID was assigned by the author because the NHRP specification was written at the same time as SCSP; PIDs are in general assigned by IANA.

SCSP puts no topological requirement on the group, though the resulting graph of NHSs must span all the servers to be synchronized.

With SCSP in use, an NHC registers with only one NHS, but it MAY use any NHS in the group.
sections.plainLanguage: All the helpers in one neighbourhood are one team with a team number. Each visitor signs in with just one helper, but can ask any helper a question.

sections.title: Leaving the Server Group
sections.content:
To prevent unlikely race conditions during updates, an NHC that wants to leave a group MUST do one of the following:

  1. send an NHRP Purge Request for itself, asking for a reply, and wait for the NHRP Purge Reply;
  2. keep the Request ID it used when registering in non-volatile RAM, and use a larger Request ID when it re-registers;
  3. not re-register for a time equal to the Holding Time given in its previous registration.

When the second method is used, the NHS the client registered with uses its own ID as the OID and the client's Request ID as the CSA Sequence Number in the CSA(S) Record.
sections.plainLanguage: When you leave the team, you have to make sure everyone knows. Either you tell them you are gone, or you write down your last ticket number so the next one is bigger, or you wait long enough that your old sign-in has expired.

sections.title: The NHRP Part of the CSA Record
sections.content:
Each SCSP CSA Record carries a client/server protocol specific part with one server's cache entry. For NHRP, the first six fields copy values from the common header of the NHRP Registration Request or Purge Request that created, deleted or changed the cache entry:

  • Address Family Number, the type of link layer addresses carried (same as ar$afn);
  • NHRP Protocol Type (same as ar$pro.type) and Snap (same as ar$pro.snap);
  • NHRP Vers Num, which is 0x01 for NHRP version 1;
  • Flags, with the U bit (the Uniqueness bit) and the A bit, which is set when the entry came from ATMARP client interaction with the NHS;
  • Request ID, the value placed in the cache entry as a result of the Registration Request, by the NHS causing the synchronization event.

The State field then gives the client's new state. Next come ten fields taken from, or derived from, the CIE of the same request: Prefix Length, Maximum Transmission Unit, Holding Time (the seconds remaining that the NHS starting the event considers the next hop NBMA information valid), Cli Addr T/L, Cli SAddr T/L, Cli Proto Len, Preference, and the variable-length client NBMA address, NBMA subaddress and protocol address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each update is like a small card that copies the details from the sign-in form: who the visitor is, where to reach them, how long the entry is good for, and whether they just arrived or left.

sections.title: Client State Values and Fixed SCSP Fields
sections.content:
The State field takes one of four values. A cache entry that merely times out does not cause a CSA Record to be sent: if everything works, all NHSs time the entry out at the same moment and act on their own.

For the protocol-independent part, the RFC fixes these values: in the Mandatory Common Part, Protocol ID 0x0002, Sender ID Len 0x04 and Recvr ID Len 0x04; in the CSAS Record, Cache Key Len 0x04 and Orig ID Len 0x04. Their meaning is described in Section B.2.0.1 and B.2.0.2 of RFC 2334.
sections.plainLanguage: A visitor can be in one of four situations, like checked in, checked in again, checked out, or never heard of. Running out of time is not announced, because every helper already knows the clock.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds no security text of its own. It says that the relevant security considerations are documented in RFC 2332 (NHRP) and RFC 2334 (SCSP).
sections.plainLanguage: This note does not add new safety rules. It points to the rules in the two bigger documents.
